question.prompt: How many three-digit positive integers have an odd number of even digits?

solutions.title: Choose the units digit last
solutions.explanation:
Once the hundreds and tens digits are chosen, the required parity of the units digit is determined. This lets us count without separating all the digit patterns.

There are \(9\) choices for the hundreds digit and \(10\) choices for the tens digit. Count the even digits among those two positions:

- If that count is \(0\) or \(2\), the units digit must be even.
- If that count is \(1\), the units digit must be odd.

There are always five choices of the required parity: \(0,2,4,6,8\) are even, and \(1,3,5,7,9\) are odd. Zero is allowed in the units position.

Every eligible number is obtained exactly once by choosing its digits this way. Thus the count is
\[
9\cdot10\cdot5=\boxed{450},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).

solutions.title: Count one or three even digits
solutions.explanation:
With three digit positions, an odd number of even digits means exactly one or exactly three. We can therefore list all allowed parity patterns.

An even hundreds digit has four choices, \(2,4,6,8\), because the first digit cannot be zero. An even tens or units digit has five choices, including zero. Each odd digit has five choices in any position.

| Hundreds | Tens | Units | Number of integers |
|---|---|---|---:|
| Even | Even | Even | \(4\cdot5\cdot5=100\) |
| Even | Odd | Odd | \(4\cdot5\cdot5=100\) |
| Odd | Even | Odd | \(5\cdot5\cdot5=125\) |
| Odd | Odd | Even | \(5\cdot5\cdot5=125\) |

The first row covers three even digits; the other rows cover each possible location of the single even digit. These patterns are disjoint and exhaustive. Adding gives
\[
100+100+125+125=\boxed{450},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).

solutions.title: Pair the numbers
solutions.explanation:
Changing only the units digit from even to odd, or from odd to even, changes the number of even digits by exactly one. We can use this to pair eligible and ineligible numbers.

Keep the hundreds and tens digits unchanged, and swap the units digit within the pairs
\[
0\leftrightarrow1,\quad
2\leftrightarrow3,\quad
4\leftrightarrow5,\quad
6\leftrightarrow7,\quad
8\leftrightarrow9.
\]
For example, \(246\) pairs with \(247\). Each pair contains one number with an odd count of even digits and one with an even count.

The swap preserves three-digit status, and applying it twice returns the original number. Thus every three-digit number belongs to exactly one pair. There are \(999-100+1=900\) three-digit positive integers, so exactly half qualify:
\[
\frac{900}{2}=\boxed{450},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
